blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Two variables are associated when the values of one tend to change in a systematic way as the values of the other change. The association is positive if they tend to rise together, negative if one tends to fall as the other rises, and absent if there is no such tendency.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Association is a description before it is a number. Ask: as one variable goes up, does the other tend to move, and in which direction? “Tend to” matters. Taller people are heavier on average, but some short people outweigh some tall ones.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Height and weight are positively associated. Hours of sunshine and a household’s heating costs are negatively associated. Shoe size and IQ in adults show no meaningful association.

points.html: An association can be linear (points scatter about a straight line; the target of Pearson’s r, §11.2), monotonic (always rising or always falling, but not necessarily straight; the target of Spearman’s and Kendall’s coefficients, §11.3) or neither. A U-shaped relationship (falling, then rising) can give a coefficient near 0 although the two variables are strongly related. Draw the scatter diagram first.
Association is not effect. Whether one variable causes the other is a separate question, taken up in §11.5–11.7.
